pos: adj. (free from guilt in a particular matter; rendering Hebrew naqi, Greek athoos)
etymology: From Latin in-, not, and nocens, harming — literally not hurting. Scripture uses it forensically: innocent of a charge, not innocent by nature.
biblical_def: Innocent in the Authorized Version is a courtroom word, not a statement about human nature. No son of Adam is innocent before God; but a man may be entirely innocent of the particular crime laid against him, and Scripture guards that innocence with extraordinary severity. The law forbids the judicial murder of the innocent outright — “the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked” (Exo 23:7) — and pronounces a covenant curse on the man who takes a bribe to do it (Deu 27:25). The shedding of innocent blood becomes the standing measure of a nation's apostasy: Manasseh filled Jerusalem with it, and of that particular sin it is written that the LORD “would not pardon” (2Ki 24:4). Jonathan pleads David's case in exactly these terms (1Sa 19:5). The word therefore does double duty in the canon: it protects the wrongly accused, and it convicts the nation that spills their blood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines innocent as free from guilt, not having done wrong or violated any law, and secondarily as harmless, doing no injury — noting its legal use for one not chargeable with the crime alleged.
webster_full: IN´NOCENT, a. Not guilty; free from guilt; not having done wrong or violated any law.
2. Free from the guilt of a particular crime or evil action.
3. Unhurtful; harmless in effects.
4. Lawful; permitted; as an innocent trade.
scriptures: Exo 23:7
Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.
Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. And all the people shall say, Amen.
And also for the innocent blood that he shed: for he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; which the LORD would not pardon.

For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?
corruption_summary: Innocence relocated from the courtroom to human nature itself — man declared innocent by default — while the actual biblical concern, the shedding of innocent blood, is renamed and defended.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern moral vocabulary treats innocence as the natural human condition, corrupted only later by circumstance or society. Scripture reverses the order entirely: men are guilty in Adam and may be innocent only of specific charges. That inversion has consequences at both ends. It removes the need for atonement, since the innocent require no ransom; and it makes conviction of sin feel like an injury done to a person rather than the truth told about him.

Meanwhile the concrete thing Scripture guards — innocent blood — is the very thing the age has learned to justify. The prophets measure a civilization by what it does to those who cannot defend themselves, and 2 Kings 24:4 records a sin of which it is said the LORD would not pardon it. Deuteronomy 27:25 puts a curse on taking payment to destroy an innocent person, and the whole congregation is required to say Amen to it. A nation that has grown comfortable with that transaction is not enlightened; it is under the twenty-seventh chapter of Deuteronomy.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqi (H5355), clean, free, acquitted — the word for innocent blood; Greek athoos (G121), unpunished, guiltless — Pilate's word as he washed his hands.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqi (H5355) — clean, exempt, acquitted; the standing phrase dam naqi, innocent blood (Deu 19:10).
Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — righteous; paired with innocent in Exo 23:7, showing the forensic register of both.
Greek athoos (G121) — guiltless, unpunished; used by Pilate of himself concerning the blood of the only truly innocent Man.
usage: “The innocent and righteous slay thou not” — the law's absolute guard on judicial murder.
“Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person” — and all the people said, Amen.
“He filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; which the LORD would not pardon” — the measure of a nation's apostasy.

pos: adj. (chargeable with an offence, liable to penalty; rendering Hebrew asham, Greek hupodikos, enochos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon gylt, a fault, crime, debt. The English word keeps the debt-sense that Scripture's trespass-offering assumes: guilt is something owed.
biblical_def: Guilty in Scripture is objective liability, not a feeling. Leviticus makes this unmistakable: a man may sin through ignorance, with the matter hidden from his own eyes, “though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity” (Lev 5:17). Guilt is a status before God's law, incurred whether or not the conscience has caught up. Joseph's brothers show the reverse case — the awakening of a guilt long carried: “We are verily guilty concerning our brother” (Gen 42:21), spoken twenty years after the deed. The divine character holds both mercy and this refusal together in one breath: the LORD forgives iniquity and transgression and sin, “and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7) — a sentence that makes the cross necessary, since God will neither leave the guilty unpunished nor abandon those He pardons. Paul's summary closes every mouth: “all the world may become guilty before God” (Rom 3:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines guilty as justly chargeable with a crime, criminal, and notes that in Scripture the word signifies liability to punishment, not merely the consciousness of wrong.
webster_full: GUILT´Y, a. Justly chargeable with a crime; not innocent.
2. Wicked; corrupt; sinful.
3. Conscious of guilt; as a guilty look.
In Scripture, guilty often signifies exposed to punishment; liable to the penalty of the law.
scriptures: Rom 3:19
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
Exo 34:7

Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation.
Lev 5:17
And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity.
And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.
corruption_summary: Guilt reclassified as a psychological injury to be relieved rather than a legal status to be pardoned — so that the gospel's answer is offered to a problem the age no longer believes it has.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic settlement treats guilt as a feeling that damages self-worth, and therefore as something to be dissolved by reframing. On that account, forgiveness is a technique for feeling better and the cross is at best a symbol of acceptance. Scripture's guilt cannot be reframed, because Leviticus 5:17 establishes that a man is guilty whether or not he knows it. A status incurred by objective violation cannot be talked away by a change in self-perception; it must be borne, either by the sinner or by a substitute.

Yet false guilt is also real, and the same doctrine cures it. Where guilt is objective, it can be objectively answered: the believer is not asked to feel less guilty but to look away from himself to a finished work. Exodus 34:7 will not clear the guilty — and that is precisely why the guilty may be cleared, since at the cross the penalty was exacted rather than waived. God did not lower the standard; He satisfied it.
roots_summary: Hebrew asham (H816), to be guilty, to incur liability — the root of the trespass-offering; Greek hupodikos (G5267), liable to judgment, literally under the sentence, in Rom 3:19.
roots_lines: Hebrew asham (H816) — to be guilty, to bear punishment; the same root names the guilt-offering, so guilt and its remedy share a word.
Greek hupodikos (G5267) — under judgment, answerable to a court; Paul's verdict on the whole world (Rom 3:19).
Greek enochos (G1777) — held in, liable; used of one guilty of the body and blood of the Lord (1Co 11:27).
usage: “Though he wist it not, yet is he guilty” — guilt is a status, not a sensation.
“That will by no means clear the guilty” — the sentence that makes substitution necessary.
“All the world may become guilty before God” — every mouth stopped.

pos: adj. (disposed to inflict suffering, pitiless; rendering Hebrew akzar, qasheh)
etymology: From Latin crudelis, from crudus, raw, bloody. The Latin root is butchery, and Scripture keeps the flavour: cruelty is rawness where mercy should be.
biblical_def: Cruel names a settled pitilessness, and Scripture's most penetrating use of it is Proverbs 12:10: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.” The point is devastating — not that the wicked lack mercy, but that even their mercies wound. What passes for kindness in an unrenewed heart is calibrated to the giver, and it damages what it touches. Jacob pronounces the same verdict on his own sons' anger: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel” (Gen 49:7) — a father cursing a disposition, not merely a deed. Solomon then supplies the self-inflicted cost: “he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh” (Pro 11:17). Cruelty is never contained to its victim. And Israel's bondage in Egypt is summed in the phrase cruel bondage (Exo 6:9), which is the estate every man is redeemed from.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cruel as disposed to give pain to others, inhuman, destitute of pity or compassion, and extends it to whatever causes pain — a cruel war, a cruel disease.
webster_full: CRU´EL, a. Disposed to give pain to others, in body or mind; willing or pleased to torment, vex or afflict; inhuman; destitute of pity, compassion or kindness.
2. Inhuman; barbarous; savage; causing pain, grief or distress.
3. Bloody; mischievous; destructive; as a cruel war.
scriptures: A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
Gen 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh.
Exo 6:9
And Moses spake so unto the children of Israel: but they hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit, and for cruel bondage.
corruption_summary: Cruelty redefined as whatever causes distress, so that telling the truth becomes cruel and flattery becomes kindness — the inversion Proverbs 12:10 already named.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has made felt distress the test of cruelty. On that measure a surgeon is crueller than a flatterer, and a faithful minister crueller than a false one. Scripture measures cruelty by outcome and disposition, not by sensation: the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel precisely because they feel like mercy and end in ruin. A doctrine that will not name sin is not gentler than one that does; it is the wicked man's tender mercy, and Proverbs has already filed it.

The corollary protects the church from the opposite error. Real cruelty exists inside religious communities — the harsh elder, the domineering husband, the discipline administered without tears — and Scripture never excuses it as faithfulness. Jacob cursed cruelty in his own household and in his own sons. Proverbs 12:10 sets the floor astonishingly low and high at once: a righteous man's mercy reaches even his livestock. Cruelty to what is beneath you is the surest index of what you are.
roots_summary: Hebrew akzar (H393), fierce, cruel, pitiless; akzari (H394), the cruel man; qasheh (H7186), hard, severe — the hardness of Egyptian bondage.
roots_lines: Hebrew akzar (H393) — cruel, fierce; used of wrath (Gen 49:7) and of the day of the LORD in the prophets.
Hebrew akzari (H394) — a cruel one; the tender mercies that are cruel in Pro 12:10.
Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, severe, obstinate; the cruel bondage of Exo 6:9, the estate of every unredeemed soul.
usage: “The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel” — even their kindness wounds.
“Cursed be their anger… for it was cruel” — Jacob curses a disposition, not just a deed.
“He that is cruel troubleth his own flesh” — cruelty is never contained to its victim.

pos: adj. and adv. (like God in disposition, devoted to God; rendering Hebrew chasid, Greek eusebos, kata theon)
etymology: From God with the Anglo-Saxon suffix -lic, like. The word means God-like in the only sense creatures may be: set apart for Him and shaped by Him.
biblical_def: Godly describes a man God has claimed and marked. David states the doctrine and its consequence in one verse: “the LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the LORD will hear when I call” (Psa 4:3) — the setting apart is God's act, and answered prayer follows from it. The Hebrew word is chasid, one who has received and reflects covenant love, so godliness is derivative by definition; it is never self-generated piety. Paul supplies the diagnostic that distinguishes it from mere religious feeling: “godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death” (2Co 7:10). Two sorrows, identical in appearance, opposite in destination. Titus grounds godly living in grace rather than effort — grace teaches us to “live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world” (Tit 2:12) — and Paul promises what it costs: “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines godly as pious, reverencing God and his character and laws, and adverbially as living in conformity to the divine law — noting godly sorrow as sorrow for sin as an offence against God.
webster_full: GOD´LY, a. Pious; reverencing God, and his character and laws.
2. Living in obedience to God's commands, from a principle of love to him and reverence of his character and precepts.
3. Pious; conformed to God's law; as a godly life.
GOD´LY, adv. Piously; righteously. 2 Tim. iii.
scriptures: Psa 4:3
But know that the LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the LORD will hear when I call unto him.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
corruption_summary: Godliness reduced to niceness or to public respectability — a manner rather than a mark — and quietly severed from the persecution Paul says always accompanies it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two counterfeits circulate. The first makes godliness a temperament: soft-spoken, agreeable, inoffensive. But agreeableness is a gift of disposition, not a fruit of the Spirit, and many an unregenerate man is pleasant. The second makes godliness a reputation to be managed, which Paul elsewhere calls a form of godliness denying the power thereof. Psalm 4:3 forecloses both by making the godly man someone God has set apart for Himself — a status conferred, then evidenced, never merely performed.

The clearest test on offer is 2 Corinthians 7:10, and it is worth pressing because the two sorrows look identical from outside. Worldly sorrow grieves consequences and terminates in death; godly sorrow grieves the offence against God and terminates in repentance no one ever regrets. The other test is 2 Timothy 3:12, which the comfortable church quietly edits: all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. Where godliness costs a man nothing at all, the word has probably been redefined.
roots_summary: Hebrew chasid (H2623), one shown covenant mercy and reflecting it; Greek eusebeia (G2150), well-directed reverence; the phrase kata theon, according to God — Paul's idiom for godly sorrow.
roots_lines: Hebrew chasid (H2623) — godly, saintly; built on chesed, covenant love, so the godly man is a loved man before he is a loving one (Psa 4:3; Psa 12:1).
Greek eusebeia (G2150) — piety, reverence rightly directed; the great mystery of godliness is God manifest in the flesh (1Ti 3:16).
Greek kata theon — according to God; Paul's phrase for the sorrow that works repentance (2Co 7:10).
usage: “The LORD hath set apart him that is godly for himself” — godliness begins as God's act.
“Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation” — two sorrows, opposite destinations.
“All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” — the promised cost.

pos: adj. (steady and careful in application; rendering Hebrew charuts, Greek spoudaios)
etymology: From Latin diligens, the present participle of diligere, to love, to choose out — so diligence is at root love applied to a task, not mere busyness.
biblical_def: Diligent describes sustained, attentive labour, and Proverbs makes it a whole doctrine of vocation. The diligent hand rules and enriches (Pro 12:24; Pro 10:4); the diligent soul is made fat (Pro 13:4); the diligent man's thoughts “tend only to plenteousness” while haste tends to want (Pro 21:5) — a distinction the modern hustle rarely observes. Diligence is not speed; it is steadiness under a chosen duty. Proverbs 22:29 promises it a hearing in high places: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings.” The word is not confined to commerce. Joshua commands diligent heed to the commandment and the law (Jos 22:5); the judges must make diligent inquisition before condemning (Deu 19:18); the psalmist makes diligent search of his own spirit in the night (Psa 77:6); and Peter commands the same energy in the soul's cultivation — “giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue” (2Pe 1:5). Diligence in Scripture is first applied to the heart, and only then to the herd.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diligent as steady in application to business, constant in effort to accomplish what is undertaken, assiduous, attentive — and notes its Scriptural application to searching and to self-examination.
webster_full: DIL´IGENT, a. Steady in application to business; constant in effort or exertion to accomplish what is undertaken; assiduous; attentive; industrious; not idle or negligent.
2. Steadily applied; prosecuted with care and constant effort; careful; assiduous; as diligent search or inquiry.
The hand of the diligent maketh rich. Prov. x.
scriptures: Pro 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
Pro 21:5
The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge;
corruption_summary: Diligence collapsed into hurry and self-promotion — the hustle that Proverbs 21:5 files under haste and assigns to want — while the diligence Scripture commands over the soul goes unpractised.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 21:5 draws a line the productivity culture cannot see: the thoughts of the diligent tend to plenteousness, but of every one that is hasty only to want. Hurry mimics diligence and produces its opposite, because diligence is thoughtful continuance and haste is anxious motion. The man who works frantically and the man who works steadily are not doing the same thing at different speeds; they are doing different things, and Scripture assigns them different ends.

The deeper loss is the object. Peter commands all diligence toward faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance — the cultivation of the soul — and Proverbs 27:23 commands the shepherd to know the state of his flocks. Both assume that the things most worth tending are the things most easily neglected while a man is busy. A believer may be scrupulously diligent in his trade and entirely slack in his own heart, and Scripture counts that man slothful where it matters.
roots_summary: Hebrew charuts (H2742), sharp, decisive, diligent — literally something cut in, the opposite of a slack hand; Greek spoude (G4710), earnest haste, zeal — Peter's all diligence.
roots_lines: Hebrew charuts (H2742) — sharp, keen, diligent; set against remiyyah, the slack or deceitful hand (Pro 10:4).
Hebrew atsel (H6102) — the sluggard; Proverbs' standing foil to the diligent (Pro 13:4).
Greek spoude (G4710) — diligence, earnestness; giving all diligence in 2Pe 1:5, the soul's cultivation.
usage: “The hand of the diligent maketh rich” — steadiness, not brilliance, is the promise.
“The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness” — and haste, only to want.
“Giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue” — the soul is the first field.

pos: adj. (submissive to authority, complying with command; rendering Hebrew shama, Greek hupekoos)
etymology: From Latin obedire, from ob-, toward, and audire, to hear. Obedience is hearing toward someone — which is exactly the Hebrew idea, where to hear and to obey are one word.
biblical_def: Obedient in Scripture is inseparable from hearing. The Hebrew shama means both, so that a man who has truly heard God has already begun to obey Him, and a man who has not obeyed has not really heard. Israel says the words at Sinai — “All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient” (Exo 24:7) — and the rest of the Old Testament is the record of what that promise was worth in fallen hands. Isaiah attaches the covenant blessing to it plainly: “If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land” (Isa 1:19), with willingness named first, since obedience without willingness is only compliance. The summit of the word is Christ: “he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Php 2:8) — the active obedience of the Son rendering what Adam and Israel could not, and imputed to all who are His. Believers are then called “obedient children” (1Pe 1:14): the obedience is not the price of sonship but the manner of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obedient as submissive to authority, yielding compliance with commands, orders or injunctions — performing what is required, or abstaining from what is forbidden.
webster_full: OBE´DIENT, a. Submissive to authority; yielding compliance with commands, orders or injunctions; performing what is required, or abstaining from what is forbid.
The chief his orders gives; the obedient band, with due observance, wait the chief's command.
In Scripture, obedience is the great test of love to God. If ye love me, keep my commandments.
scriptures: Exo 24:7
And he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient.
Isa 1:19
If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land:
Php 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
As obedient children, not fashioning yourselves according to the former lusts in your ignorance:
corruption_summary: Obedience treated as an insult to the autonomous self — submission reframed as weakness or abuse — so that the one posture creatures owe their Maker is renamed a pathology.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of the age is autonomy: a self that authors its own law and owes no prior obedience to anyone. Against that, every biblical use of the word is an offence, and the offence is deliberate. Creatures obey; that is what it means to be a creature. Isaiah 1:19 refuses even the modern escape of grudging compliance by naming willingness first — God is not after the behaviour minus the heart, which is why Sinai's we will do, and be obedient could be sincerely said and still fail.

Where authority has genuinely been abused, the corruption feeds on real wounds, and the church must not be careless here. But the answer is not the abolition of obedience; it is the recovery of its Object and its pattern. Philippians 2:8 shows obedience in the Son of God Himself, freely rendered to the point of the cross — obedience that is neither servile nor coerced, and that saves those who could never render it. And 1 Peter 1:14 orders it rightly: obedient children. Sonship first, obedience as its manner.
roots_summary: Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear, and thereby to obey; Greek hupakouo (G5219), to hear under, to answer a knock; hupekoos (G5255), obedient — used of Christ in Php 2:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, listen, obey; the Shema itself is a command to hear, and hearing is not complete until it acts (Deu 6:4).
Greek hupakouo (G5219) — to listen attentively, submit; literally to hear from under, from the posture of one placed beneath.
Greek hupekoos (G5255) — obedient; used three times in the New Testament, the weightiest of Christ obedient unto death (Php 2:8).
usage: “All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient” — sincerely said at Sinai, and beyond fallen strength.
“If ye be willing and obedient” — willingness named first; God is not after behaviour minus heart.
“Became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” — the obedience that saves.

pos: adj. (destitute of knowledge; rendering Hebrew ba'ar, Greek agnoeo, idiotes)
etymology: From Latin ignorans, not knowing, from in-, not, and gnarus, knowing. Scripture distinguishes sharply between innocent lack of learning and culpable refusal to know.
biblical_def: Ignorant carries two very different weights in Scripture. There is ignorance that is no sin at all: Peter and John were reckoned “unlearned and ignorant men” by the council, and the text turns the insult into a commendation — “they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13). Formal learning is not godliness, and its absence is not disqualification. But there is also a culpable ignorance which Scripture treats as guilt: Israel, “being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness” (Rom 10:3) — ignorance that is a form of self-assertion, not of innocence. Isaiah's watchmen are the worst case: blind, ignorant, “dumb dogs, they cannot bark” (Isa 56:10), shepherds ignorant of the very danger they were posted to announce. Asaph, meanwhile, models the honest confession of it — “So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee” (Psa 73:22) — said not of his schooling but of his envy of the wicked.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ignorant as destitute of knowledge, uninstructed or uninformed, and notes the sense of being unacquainted with a particular thing — distinguishing want of instruction from want of understanding.
webster_full: IG´NORANT, a. Destitute of knowledge; uninstructed or uninformed; untaught; unenlightened.
2. Unacquainted with; unknowing; as ignorant of the passage.
3. Unknown; undiscovered; a sense not now in use.
4. Done through ignorance; as an ignorant error.
scriptures: Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Rom 10:3
For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.
His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.
corruption_summary: Credentials mistaken for competence in the things of God, so that the unlearned believer is silenced — while the culpable ignorance Scripture actually condemns, ignorance of God's righteousness, goes unnoticed in the learned.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4:13 is a permanent rebuke to intellectual gatekeeping in the church. The council's assessment was accurate — these men were unlearned — and entirely beside the point, because they had been with Jesus. Wherever the ordinary believer is taught that Scripture is too difficult for him without a scholar's mediation, the Reformation's recovery of the open Bible is being quietly reversed, and the priesthood of all believers with it.

The opposite abuse is to make ignorance a virtue and study a suspicion, which Scripture never does. The ignorance it condemns is not unlettered but willful: Romans 10:3 describes men with every advantage of Scripture who did not know God's righteousness because they were busy constructing their own. That ignorance is compatible with immense learning. Isaiah's watchmen were the qualified men, and their qualification is precisely what makes their silence damnable.
roots_summary: Hebrew ba'ar (H1198), brutish, like a beast — Asaph's self-description; Greek agnoeo (G50), not to know; idiotes (G2399), a private unskilled man — the council's word for the apostles.
roots_lines: Hebrew ba'ar (H1198) — brutish, stupid as cattle; Asaph's confession that envy had reduced him to a beast before God (Psa 73:22).
Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant, not to understand; Paul's repeated I would not have you ignorant makes doctrine a pastoral duty (Rom 11:25; 1Co 10:1).
Greek idiotes (G2399) — a private person, unskilled, a layman; applied to Peter and John by the Sanhedrin (Act 4:13).
usage: “Unlearned and ignorant men… they had been with Jesus” — the insult becomes the commendation.
“Being ignorant of God's righteousness” — the ignorance that is self-assertion.
“They are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs” — watchmen who cannot bark.

pos: adj. (surpassing, of great worth; rendering Hebrew addir, yaqar, Greek diaphoros, kreitton)
etymology: From Latin excellens, rising above, towering. In the Authorized Version the word belongs first to God, and only derivatively to anything else.
biblical_def: Excellent is chiefly a word about God in Scripture, and its most familiar use is a psalm that begins and ends with it: “O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!” (Psa 8:1, 9). The excellency belongs to the Name, to the lovingkindness (Psa 36:7), and to the greatness for which He is praised (Psa 150:2) — and where the word is applied to creatures it is applied to those in whom God has put something of Himself: “the saints that are in the earth, and… the excellent, in whom is all my delight” (Psa 16:3). David's delight rests where God's does. Hebrews takes the comparative and makes it the engine of the whole epistle — a more excellent name than the angels (Heb 1:4), a more excellent sacrifice than Cain's (Heb 11:4) — teaching Christian excellence not as achievement but as comparison: what is better, and why. Psalm 141:5 gives the most bracing use of all, calling a righteous man's rebuke “an excellent oil, which shall not break my head.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excellent as being of great virtue or worth, eminent or distinguished for what is amiable or valuable — and notes that applied to God it denotes perfection above all comparison.
webster_full: EX´CELLENT, a. Being of great virtue or worth; eminent or distinguished for what is amiable, valuable or laudable.
2. Being of great value or use, applied to things; remarkable for good properties.
3. Distinguished for superior attainments; as an excellent artist.
4. Consummate; complete; in an ill sense.
scriptures: Psa 8:1
To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of David. O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth! who hast set thy glory above the heavens.
Psa 16:3
But to the saints that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight.
Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities.
Heb 11:4
By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.
corruption_summary: Excellence detached from its Source and turned into a performance metric — the church borrowing the language of production values while Scripture reserves the word for God and for what He has made better.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live danger is not that the world has redefined excellence but that the church has imported a merely professional version of it. Where excellence names production values, platform quality, and organizational polish, a congregation can be excellent by every measure it tracks and never once display the thing Psalm 8 means. The principle to recover is that excellence in Scripture is first a divine attribute and only then a derived one.

Psalm 141:5 supplies the corrective that no performance culture can absorb: the righteous man's rebuke is excellent oil. A community serious about excellence in the biblical sense will therefore prize correction above applause, and will measure itself by Hebrews' comparative — is this better, and better by what standard? Abel's sacrifice was more excellent than Cain's not because it was better executed but because it was offered in faith.
roots_summary: Hebrew addir (H117), majestic, mighty — the excellent Name of Psalm 8; yaqar (H3368), precious; Greek diaphoros (G1313), differing, hence superior; kreitton (G2909), better — the key word of Hebrews.
roots_lines: Hebrew addir (H117) — majestic, glorious, mighty; how excellent is thy name (Psa 8:1), and the excellent ones of Psa 16:3.
Hebrew tob (H2896) with comparative force — the psalmist's excellent oil of a righteous rebuke (Psa 141:5).
Greek kreitton (G2909) — better, more excellent; the structural word of Hebrews, comparing Christ to every shadow that preceded Him (Heb 1:4).
usage: “How excellent is thy name in all the earth!” — the word belongs first to God.
“The excellent, in whom is all my delight” — David's delight rests where God's does.
“Let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil” — correction prized above applause.

pos: adj. (becoming, seemly, of pleasing form; rendering Hebrew naveh, ta'ar, Greek euschemon)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon cymlic, becoming, suitable. The Authorized Version keeps the older sense: comely means fitting first and beautiful second.
biblical_def: Comely means becoming — what suits, what is fitting to the thing itself. Its most important use is liturgical: “Rejoice in the LORD, O ye righteous: for praise is comely for the upright” (Psa 33:1), and again, “it is pleasant; and praise is comely” (Psa 147:1). Praise is not merely permitted to the redeemed; it fits them, as clothing fits a body. The word also carries plain physical beauty — David is described as “a comely person” before Saul ever sees him (1Sa 16:18) — and the Song of Solomon uses it repeatedly of the bride, most famously in her own honest confession, “I am black, but comely” (Sng 1:5). That verse holds the two senses together: an appearance the world would discount, and a comeliness the Bridegroom sees and names. Read typologically, as the Reformed tradition has always read the Song, it is the church's own testimony — unlovely in herself, comely in Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comely as handsome, graceful, symmetrical, and also as decent, suitable, proper — noting that what is comely is what becomes the person or the occasion.
webster_full: COME´LY, a. Properly, becoming; suitable.
2. Handsome; graceful; as a comely youth; a person of comely looks.
3. Decent; suitable; proper; becoming; as comely apparel.
COME´LY, adv. Handsomely; decently; in a becoming manner.
scriptures: Psa 33:1
Rejoice in the LORD, O ye righteous: for praise is comely for the upright.
Praise ye the LORD: for it is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely.
Sng 1:5
I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon.

Then answered one of the servants, and said, Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him.
corruption_summary: Beauty severed from fitness — comeliness reduced to appearance and appearance to appetite — while the biblical sense, that praise becomes the redeemed, is largely forgotten in worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern eye reads comely as merely pretty, and so loses the word's spine. Comeliness is fitness: the right thing in the right place, which is why the Authorized Version can call praise comely and apparel comely in the same breath. Once beauty is cut loose from fitness it has nothing left to be measured by except desire, and a culture that has taken that step will produce both the objectification it complains of and the endless dissatisfaction that follows it.

In worship the loss is sharpest. Psalm 33:1 does not say praise is required of the upright but that it becomes them — it is the fitting garment of a righteous man, as natural to him as speech. Congregational singing that has to be coaxed has usually forgotten this. And Song of Solomon 1:5, read as the church's confession, sets the whole matter right: I am black, but comely. The comeliness is real, and it is not self-generated.
roots_summary: Hebrew naveh (H5000), comely, becoming — used of praise and of the bride; ta'ar (H8389), form, figure; Greek euschemon (G2158), of good form, seemly.
roots_lines: Hebrew naveh (H5000) — comely, seemly, befitting; praise is comely for the upright (Psa 33:1) and the bride is comely (Sng 1:5).
Hebrew ta'ar (H8389) — outline, form, figure; the physical comeliness noted of David (1Sa 16:18).
Greek euschemon (G2158) — well-formed, becoming, honourable; Paul's word for the comely parts of the body in 1Co 12:24.
usage: “Praise is comely for the upright” — praise fits the redeemed as clothing fits a body.
“I am black, but comely” — the church's confession: unlovely in herself, comely in Him.
“A comely person, and the LORD is with him” — and the second clause is the one that mattered.

pos: adj. (not righteous, acting contrary to right; rendering Hebrew avval, Greek adikos)
etymology: From un-, not, and Latin justus, according to law or right. The biblical word is not about unfairness felt but about righteousness violated.
biblical_def: Unjust is the settled biblical name for a man out of line with God's righteousness. Proverbs states the mutual repugnance flatly: “An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked” (Pro 29:27) — the antipathy runs both ways and cannot be negotiated away. Zephaniah adds the terrible mark of the hardened: “the unjust knoweth no shame” (Zep 3:5). The Lord Jesus uses the word to expose the small scale on which character is actually revealed — “he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10) — and to describe God's common grace, which falls indiscriminately: He “sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust” (Mat 5:45). All of it converges on one verse where the unjust are not merely condemned but rescued: “Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1Pe 3:18). That is the gospel in the vocabulary of this entry — the only Just One, in the place of the unjust.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unjust as acting contrary to the standard of right, not doing to others what the law of God or man requires — and as contrary to justice and right, applied to things.
webster_full: UNJUST´, a. Acting contrary to the standard of right established by the divine law; not equitable; wrongful.
2. Contrary to justice and right; wrongful; as an unjust sentence; unjust demands.
3. Not just; partial; as an unjust judge.
4. Dishonest; as unjust gain.
scriptures: For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:
An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
Mat 5:45
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
corruption_summary: Justice redefined as the redistribution of outcomes by group, so that unjust now names any disparity — a standard external to Scripture, applied to Scripture, and finding it wanting.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant frameworks of the age locate injustice in group outcomes and define the unjust as whoever benefits from a disparity. The biblical category is different in kind: injustice is a relation to God's law, committed by persons, and Scripture's own remedies are correspondingly personal — honest weights, impartial courts, wages paid the same day, no respect of persons for rich or poor alike. Leviticus explicitly forbids partiality toward the poor man in judgment as well as toward the great, which no theory built on group standing can accommodate.

This is not indifference to the oppressed; the prophets are ferocious on their behalf, and a church that ignores them has abandoned the text. But the biblical categories are the widow, the orphan, the stranger, the hired servant — concrete persons with concrete claims — not abstract classes. And the decisive verse is 1 Peter 3:18, which forecloses self-righteousness on every side: the just for the unjust. Everyone who reads that sentence rightly finds himself named in the second half of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew avval (H5767), one who does perversity; avel (H5766), injustice, wrong; Greek adikos (G94), the alpha-privative of dike, right — literally the un-righted man.
roots_lines: Hebrew avel (H5766) — injustice, unrighteousness, wrong; the covenant courts' standing prohibition, ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment (Lev 19:15).
Greek adikos (G94) — unjust, unrighteous; the unjust steward (Luk 16:8) and the unjust for whom the Just One suffered (1Pe 3:18).
Greek dikaios (G1342) — just, righteous; the direct antonym, and the title of Christ in 1Pe 3:18.
usage: “The just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” — the gospel in this entry's vocabulary.
“He that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” — character shows at small scale.
“The unjust knoweth no shame” — the mark of the hardened.
